name: GABON

flag.title: Flag of Gabon
flag.note: Green, yellow & blue — forest, sun, ocean

lead: Gabon sits on Africa's Atlantic coast where the Equator runs through ancient rainforest. Over 80% of its land is jungle — sheltering forest elephants, silverback gorillas, and the mandrill, the world's most colourful monkey. Gabon has kept most of its trees standing, making it one of the planet's greatest carbon-absorbing green lungs.

facts.label: Land area
facts.sub: about the size of New Zealand

sections.geography: A forest on the ocean's edge

geo: Gabon straddles the Equator on Central Africa's Atlantic coast. Thick rainforest blankets over 80% of the land, threaded by the mighty Ogooué River — Gabon's highway for centuries — winding 1,200 km to the sea.

The coast swaps between white-sand beaches, mangrove swamps, and rocky coves. Inland, hills rise to the Chaillu Massif, where Lopé National Park holds ancient savanna ringed by jungle — a rare mix that UNESCO declared a world wonder.
animals: Gabon shelters nearly 85,000 forest elephants — more than any other country. In Loango National Park you can watch them strolling along the beach, waves lapping at their feet, while hippos body-surf in the surf nearby.

The mandrill, the world's largest monkey with a vivid red-and-blue face, is Gabon's national animal. Around 35,000 western lowland gorillas live in the forests, and Lopé hosts the world's biggest recorded mandrill troop — over 1,400 strong.
culture: Gabon has more than 40 ethnic groups, the largest being the Fang. The Bwiti spiritual tradition weaves ancestor veneration, polyrhythmic drumming, and the sacred iboga plant — a rainforest shrub now studied worldwide as a potential addiction medicine.

Music fills village life: the mvet harp-lute and wooden obala xylophone set the beat at festivals. Meals mix French influence with forest flavours — smoked fish, cassava, plantain, and fresh lobster along the coast.
history: Portuguese sailors arrived in 1472 and named the estuary 'Gabão' for its cloak-like shape. France colonised it in the 1800s; Libreville was founded by freed enslaved people — its name literally means 'free town'.

Gabon won independence on 17 August 1960. Oil wealth in the 1970s made it one of Africa's richer nations. In 2021 it became the first African country paid cash — $17 million — for protecting its forests under the UN REDD+ programme.
wows: Gabon absorbs more CO₂ than it produces — one of few countries on Earth that is a net carbon sink.
In Loango you can see elephants on the beach, hippos surfing, and offshore whales — all on the same day.
The iboga plant, declared a national treasure in 2000, is now studied as a treatment for drug addiction.
In 2002 Gabon created 13 national parks at once, protecting 11% of its land in a single conservation move.
Forest elephants are Gabon's 'mega-gardeners', scattering seeds across vast distances inside their dung.
Lopé holds 1,800 ancient rock carvings alongside gorillas — a rare UNESCO natural and cultural site.
Gabon's flag has a rare 3:4 ratio — shared by only DR Congo, Papua New Guinea, and San Marino.

myths.myth: Gabon is just jungle with nothing else
myths.fact: Gabon has a modern capital with skyscrapers and was one of Africa's wealthiest countries per person, sitting firmly in the upper-middle-income bracket.

myths.myth: All African elephants are the same
myths.fact: Gabon's forest elephant is a separate species — smaller, with straighter tusks, living deep in jungle far from the savanna elephants most people picture.
